questions.q: How does the 3-qubit bit-flip code encode a data qubit |psi> = a|0> + b|1>?
options: Via two CNOT gates (qubit1->qubit2, qubit1->qubit3), producing the entangled state a|000> + b|111>
By measuring the qubit and writing the classical result onto two ancilla qubits
By applying a Hadamard gate to each of 3 separate copies of the qubit
By cloning the qubit three times using a dedicated cloning circuit
questions.explain: The encoding circuit is exactly two CNOTs, entangling the 3 qubits into a|000> + b|111> without ever cloning the unknown state a and b.

questions.q: What are the stabilizer generators of the 3-qubit bit-flip code?
options: Z1Z2 and Z2Z3
X1X2 and X2X3
Z1Z2Z3 only
X1 and X2 and X3 individually
questions.explain: The bit-flip code's stabilizers are Z1Z2 and Z2Z3 -- both equal +1 on the valid encoded states a|000>+b|111>, and detect disagreements caused by X errors.

questions.q: According to the verified syndrome table, what correction does a syndrome of (Z1Z2, Z2Z3) = (1,1) indicate (starting from logical |000>)?
options: An X error occurred on qubit 2 -- flip qubit 2 to correct
No error occurred
An X error occurred on qubit 1
An X error occurred on qubit 3
questions.explain: The verified table shows errorPos=1 (qubit 2) produces state 010 and syndrome 11, uniquely identifying qubit 2 as the one to flip back.

questions.q: Why can't the 3-qubit bit-flip code detect a Z (phase-flip) error on one of its qubits?
options: A Z error doesn't change any computational-basis bit value, so it produces no disagreement in Z1Z2 or Z2Z3, leaving the syndrome at 00 as if nothing happened
Z errors are physically impossible on qubits encoded this way
The code actually does detect Z errors, using the same syndrome table
Z errors always produce a syndrome of 11, identical to a qubit-2 bit-flip
questions.explain: Z1Z2 and Z2Z3 are built to catch disagreements in computational-basis values; a phase error leaves those values untouched, so it passes through undetected -- exactly why a separate phase-flip code (next lesson) is needed.

questions.q: Why is the encoded state a|000> + b|111> described as 'entangled' rather than as 'three copies of the qubit'?
options: No single one of the 3 qubits alone holds the values a and b -- the information is distributed across correlations between all 3 qubits
Entanglement and copying are the same concept, just different names
Because the ancilla qubits start in the |1> state instead of |0>
Because CNOT gates always destroy superposition
questions.explain: Unlike literal copies (which would each individually reproduce a|0>+b|1>), the entangled state a|000>+b|111> only reveals a and b jointly across all 3 qubits -- consistent with no-cloning.
